factStatement: Machine learning is one way of building artificial intelligence, and deep learning is one way of doing machine learning.
familyName: Placing the three terms inside one another
measurementObjective: Given the three terms, say which contains which.
distractorStrategy: The nesting reversed, with artificial intelligence placed inside machine learning; the three offered as separate fields that do not overlap; deep learning equated with the whole of the subject.
notes: The widest entry point. Keep it about scope rather than about what any of them can do.

factStatement: A rule-based system does what someone wrote down; a learned system does what its examples supported.
familyName: Deciding whether a system was written or trained
measurementObjective: Given a described system, say whether its behaviour was programmed or learned from examples.
distractorStrategy: Any system that behaves cleverly assumed to be learned — a spell checker with a word list is the productive case; a learned system called rule-based because its output is consistent.
notes: At least one stem should be a rule-based system that looks intelligent, since that is where the assumption shows.

factStatement: Training data is the examples a system generalises from; it is not a store the system looks answers up in.
familyName: Recognising what training data does
measurementObjective: Given a description of training, say what the examples were used for.
distractorStrategy: Training data treated as a lookup table the system consults at use time — the single commonest model students hold; examples treated as instructions written by hand.

conceptName: What kind of question is being asked
factStatement: Sorting things into named categories, predicting a number, and grouping without categories are three different tasks.
familyName: Naming the shape of a described task
measurementObjective: Given a task in plain words, say whether it sorts into categories, predicts a quantity, or groups without them.
distractorStrategy: A prediction of a number described as sorting into categories, and the reverse; grouping confused with sorting, which differs only in whether the categories were named in advance.

conceptName: What kind of question is being asked
factStatement: A task where the right answer is recorded for each example is a different problem from one where it is not.
familyName: Deciding whether the examples carry answers
measurementObjective: Given a described collection of data, say whether it already contains the answers a system would learn from.
distractorStrategy: Data assumed to carry answers because it is well organised; answers assumed absent because nobody wrote them deliberately, where past outcomes supply them.
notes: Historical outcomes as accidental answers is the case worth asking about — a record of which customers left is a set of answers nobody set out to create.

conceptName: When learning is the wrong tool
factStatement: A task whose rule is already known and can be written down does not need a system to discover it.
familyName: Deciding whether a task needs learning at all
measurementObjective: Given a task, say whether it calls for a learned system or a written rule.
distractorStrategy: Learning chosen for a task with an exact known rule — computing tax, validating a checksum; a written rule chosen for a task nobody can state, such as recognising a handwritten digit.
notes: Both errors must appear across the family, or it teaches that one answer is always right.

conceptName: What comes out of the examples
factStatement: A system can only pick up distinctions its examples actually contain.
familyName: Reasoning about what a set of examples supports
measurementObjective: Given a described set of examples, say what a system could and could not learn to tell apart.
distractorStrategy: A distinction the examples never contained assumed learnable; a distinction present in the examples denied because it was not the stated purpose.

conceptName: What comes out of the examples
factStatement: Behaviour on inputs unlike anything in the examples is not predictable from performance on inputs like them.
familyName: Predicting behaviour on an unfamiliar input
measurementObjective: Given how a system performed on its examples, say what follows about an input unlike them.
distractorStrategy: Performance assumed to carry over to any input; the system assumed to refuse or to signal doubt, where a confident wrong answer is the usual outcome.
notes: That the system answers confidently rather than declining is the point; a stem should make the unfamiliarity concrete rather than abstract.

factStatement: A high proportion correct can be achieved by ignoring a rare case entirely.
familyName: Reasoning about what an accuracy figure reports
measurementObjective: Given an accuracy figure and the makeup of the data, say what the figure does and does not establish.
distractorStrategy: A 99 per cent figure accepted as strong where 99 per cent of cases share one answer; the figure rejected as meaningless, which overcorrects.
notes: The rare-disease shape is the canonical stem and the arithmetic must stay trivial.

conceptName: What a trained system cannot do
factStatement: A learned system produces an answer; it does not thereby produce a reason, and any reason it states is another output rather than a record of its working.
familyName: Reasoning about what a trained system can be asked for
measurementObjective: Given a request made of a trained system, say whether the system can supply it.
distractorStrategy: A stated reason accepted as the real cause of the answer; the system assumed unable to produce any explanation at all, which is also wrong.

conceptName: When the examples were the problem
factStatement: A group absent from the examples is a group the system was never asked to handle.
familyName: Tracing a failure back to the examples
measurementObjective: Given a system failing on a particular kind of input, decide whether the examples explain it.
distractorStrategy: The method blamed where the data is at fault; more data of the same kind proposed as the fix, which does not close the gap.

conceptName: When the examples were the problem
factStatement: A system will use whatever distinguishes the examples, including something that has nothing to do with the task.
familyName: Identifying a system that learned the wrong thing
measurementObjective: Given a system that scores well and fails in use, identify the incidental signal it used.
distractorStrategy: Insufficient data proposed where the data was plentiful and misleading; the signal named in a way that would also have been present in the failing cases.
notes: The stem must supply the incidental difference, or the item becomes a guess about the world.

factStatement: A system measured on the same examples it learned from reports how well it memorised, not how well it will do.
familyName: Judging whether a measurement was worth taking
measurementObjective: Given how a system was measured, say what the resulting figure supports.
distractorStrategy: A perfect score on the training examples read as strong evidence; every measurement dismissed, which leaves nothing usable; the size of the data offered as the deciding factor.

factStatement: Whether to write rules or learn from examples is settled by whether the rule is known, whether examples exist, and whether a wrong answer is tolerable.
familyName: Choosing between rules and learning for a stated requirement
measurementObjective: Given a requirement with stated constraints, choose the approach that meets it.
distractorStrategy: Learning chosen where the requirement demands an auditable reason for every decision; rules chosen where nobody can state the rule; an approach that is right in general and wrong under the stated constraint.
notes: Every option must be defensible under some requirement; the stem must state the one that settles it.

factStatement: Asking where a system got its behaviour, what its examples contained and how it was measured works on a system nobody has described in those terms.
familyName: Judging an unfamiliar system from how it was built
measurementObjective: Given a system the student has not met, work out what its described construction permits and forbids.
distractorStrategy: A conclusion that would follow for a different construction; a capability assumed from the system being described as intelligent; a limit asserted that the stated construction does not impose.
notes: No stem may name a real product — the construction is stated in the question and the reasoning is the measurement.

conceptName: What the text is broken into
factStatement: A model handles text as pieces that are often smaller than a word, not as characters and not as whole words.
familyName: Recognising what the pieces are
measurementObjective: Given a description of how text is processed, say what the unit is.
distractorStrategy: Characters and whole words offered as the unit, which are the two natural guesses; sentences offered for students who reason from meaning rather than mechanism.
notes: Keep this about the existence of a unit rather than about any particular scheme, which varies between systems.

factStatement: A model responds to the text currently in front of it, and has no access to anything outside it.
familyName: Recognising what is in front of the model
measurementObjective: Given a described situation, say what the model can and cannot see.
distractorStrategy: The model assumed to see files, screens or earlier separate conversations; the model assumed to see nothing but the last message, which is also wrong.

conceptName: Training and use are different times
factStatement: Training happens once, before use; answering a question is not training and changes nothing about the model.
familyName: Separating training from use
measurementObjective: Given a described event, say whether it is training or use.
distractorStrategy: A correction offered during a conversation assumed to have taught the model — the single most common belief; use assumed to be training because the model improves within one conversation.
notes: Improving within a conversation is real and is explained by the context, not by learning; that distinction is the item.

factStatement: Output is produced piece by piece, each chosen given everything written so far, rather than planned whole and then written out.
familyName: Reasoning about how an answer is assembled
measurementObjective: Given a described output, say what the manner of its production explains.
distractorStrategy: The model assumed to know its own conclusion before writing it; the process assumed to be retrieval from a store of prepared answers.

factStatement: The same prompt can produce different answers because the next piece is selected from several possibilities rather than fixed.
familyName: Explaining why two answers differ
measurementObjective: Given two different answers to one prompt, say what accounts for the difference.
distractorStrategy: The model assumed to have changed between the two; the difference blamed on the prompt having been altered; the difference treated as proof that one answer is wrong.

factStatement: The context holds a limited amount, and once it is full the earliest material stops being visible.
familyName: Predicting what happens as the context fills
measurementObjective: Given a long exchange, say what the model can still see and what it cannot.
distractorStrategy: The model assumed to summarise rather than lose the earliest material; the loss assumed to be announced; the whole conversation assumed to persist indefinitely.
notes: That the loss is silent is the part worth measuring, since a warned loss would be a different problem.

conceptName: Training and use are different times
factStatement: Anything established within one conversation is held in the context and is gone when the context is.
familyName: Deciding what survives a conversation
measurementObjective: Given something established in one conversation, say whether it is available in another.
distractorStrategy: A correction assumed to persist for other users; a preference assumed to persist for the same user; nothing assumed to persist even within the one conversation.
notes: Products may add a memory feature on top; the stem must state whether one is present so the mechanism is what is measured.

factStatement: Events after training are unknown to the model unless they are supplied in the context.
familyName: Deciding whether a question is answerable from training
measurementObjective: Given a question, say whether the model could know the answer and what would be needed if not.
distractorStrategy: The model assumed to say it does not know, where a confident guess is the usual result; the model assumed unable to answer even when the material is supplied in the prompt.

conceptName: What good writing does not prove
factStatement: How confident and well written an answer is says nothing about whether it is true, because both are produced the same way.
familyName: Judging what the manner of an answer establishes
measurementObjective: Given an answer described by its manner, say what follows about its accuracy.
distractorStrategy: Confidence read as evidence; hedging read as evidence of falsity, which is the same error mirrored; detail read as evidence, though detail is exactly what fabrication supplies.
notes: The mirrored error matters — a student who distrusts only hedged answers has not learned the point.

factStatement: How freely the next piece is chosen can be adjusted, trading variety against repeatability.
familyName: Reasoning about a setting that changes variability
measurementObjective: Given a requirement for repeatable or varied output, say which direction the setting should move.
distractorStrategy: Reduced variability assumed to guarantee correctness; the setting assumed to make the model more capable rather than more repeatable.
notes: Described by behaviour rather than by any parameter name, so the item does not date.

factStatement: A model that contradicts something established much earlier in a long exchange has probably lost it from the context.
familyName: Diagnosing an answer that ignores what was said
measurementObjective: Given an exchange where the model contradicts an earlier instruction, identify the likely cause.
distractorStrategy: The model accused of refusing or of disagreeing; the instruction assumed to have been misunderstood, where the stem shows it was followed for a time.
notes: The instruction must have been obeyed earlier in the stem, or loss cannot be distinguished from misunderstanding.

factStatement: An answer that was true when the model was trained and is no longer true is a different fault from an invented one, and needs a different remedy.
familyName: Distinguishing an out-of-date answer from an invented one
measurementObjective: Given a wrong answer, decide whether it is out of date or fabricated, and what would settle it.
distractorStrategy: Every wrong answer classed as invention; a fabricated answer excused as merely out of date; the remedy for one applied to the other.

factStatement: What a model can be relied on for follows from how it produces text, not from how well it writes.
familyName: Deriving a limit from the mechanism
measurementObjective: Given a described use, say whether the mechanism supports it and why.
distractorStrategy: A limit asserted that the mechanism does not impose; a capability assumed because the output looked right once; the answer resting on a product feature rather than on the mechanism.

conceptName: When to reach for something else
factStatement: A task needing an exact, checkable and repeatable answer is better served by something that computes it than by something that generates it.
familyName: Deciding whether a generative model fits the task
measurementObjective: Given a task with stated requirements, decide whether generation is the right approach.
distractorStrategy: Generation chosen for arithmetic, for an authoritative lookup, or for anything requiring the same answer every time; generation rejected for drafting, which it suits.
notes: Both directions must appear, or the family teaches suspicion rather than judgement.

factStatement: A behaviour nobody has explained can usually be accounted for by the context, the training time, or the way the next piece is chosen.
familyName: Explaining an unfamiliar behaviour from the mechanism
measurementObjective: Given a behaviour the student has not met, choose the account of it the mechanism supports.
distractorStrategy: An account requiring the model to have intentions; an account requiring it to have learned during use; an account that would explain a different behaviour than the one described.
notes: Behaviours are described plainly and never attributed to a named product.

conceptName: What a request has to contain
factStatement: A prompt that names a topic without saying what to do with it leaves the task unstated.
familyName: Recognising whether a request states a task
measurementObjective: Given several prompts, say which one states what is actually wanted.
distractorStrategy: A topic offered as a task; a long prompt assumed to state a task because it is detailed; a polite framing mistaken for an instruction.
notes: Length must not correlate with the key anywhere in this skill, or the family measures reading stamina.

conceptName: What a request has to contain
factStatement: Anything needed to do the task that the reader could not know has to be stated.
familyName: Recognising context a request has left out
measurementObjective: Given a prompt, identify what the responder would have to guess.
distractorStrategy: Something already stated named as missing; something genuinely irrelevant named as missing; the missing item named at the wrong level of detail.

conceptName: Saying what the answer should look like
factStatement: The shape of the output is part of the request and can be specified as precisely as the content.
familyName: Recognising an instruction about the shape of the answer
measurementObjective: Given a prompt, say which part of it constrains the form of the output.
distractorStrategy: A constraint on content mistaken for one on form; a request for brevity treated as a format; a stated audience treated as a format.

conceptName: Requests that can be read two ways
factStatement: A prompt open to two readings will be answered under one of them, and not necessarily the intended one.
familyName: Finding the request that could be read two ways
measurementObjective: Given several prompts, identify the one with two defensible readings and say what they are.
distractorStrategy: A prompt called ambiguous because it is brief; a genuinely ambiguous prompt passed over because it reads naturally; the two readings stated so that only one is defensible.
notes: Both readings must be genuinely available from the words, so a reader can verify the answer from the text.

factStatement: A constraint states which otherwise reasonable answers are unacceptable.
familyName: Working out what a constraint excludes
measurementObjective: Given a prompt with a constraint, say which candidate answers it rules out.
distractorStrategy: An answer excluded that the constraint permits; an answer admitted that it forbids; the constraint read as a preference rather than a requirement.

factStatement: An example in a request shows the form wanted, and is copied in shape rather than in content.
familyName: Predicting what an example in a request does
measurementObjective: Given a prompt containing an example, say what the example will and will not carry over.
distractorStrategy: The example assumed to be reproduced verbatim; the example assumed to be ignored; a single example assumed to establish a pattern it does not determine.
notes: One stem should carry an example whose shape is ambiguous, so that one example is genuinely not enough.

factStatement: Adding detail removes unwanted answers and can also remove wanted ones.
familyName: Predicting the effect of adding detail to a request
measurementObjective: Given a prompt and a proposed addition, say how the range of acceptable answers changes.
distractorStrategy: More detail assumed always better; the addition assumed to have no effect; an addition that narrows content described as narrowing form.

conceptName: Saying what the answer should look like
factStatement: A format specified precisely enough to be checked mechanically is worth more than one described loosely.
familyName: Choosing a format the output can be checked against
measurementObjective: Given a downstream use, choose the format specification that makes the output usable.
distractorStrategy: A vague instruction to be concise offered as a format; a format that is precise and does not suit the downstream use; a format so rigid it excludes the content.

conceptName: Requests that ask too much at once
factStatement: A prompt containing several tasks tends to be answered well for some of them and thinly for the rest.
familyName: Deciding how to split a request that asks too much
measurementObjective: Given a compound request, choose the split that lets each part be judged.
distractorStrategy: A split that separates parts which depend on each other; a split along the wrong seam, leaving one part still compound; no split, on the grounds that context is lost.

factStatement: The same question has different correct answers for a beginner, a specialist and a decision maker.
familyName: Reasoning about the effect of naming an audience
measurementObjective: Given a request and a stated audience, say which candidate answer fits.
distractorStrategy: An answer correct for a different audience; an answer that is simply shorter, with simplicity mistaken for suitability; the audience treated as a matter of tone alone.

conceptName: Why an answer came out wrong
factStatement: An output that misses the point can usually be traced to one thing the prompt failed to state.
familyName: Tracing an unsatisfactory answer back to the request
measurementObjective: Given a prompt and a disappointing output, identify the part of the prompt responsible.
distractorStrategy: The model blamed where the prompt is at fault; a real omission named that does not explain this particular output; the fault located in a part of the prompt that was obeyed.
notes: The output must be described specifically enough that only one omission accounts for it.

conceptName: Why an answer came out wrong
factStatement: Constraints can combine to rule out every acceptable answer, and the result is a poor answer rather than a refusal.
familyName: Finding the constraint that made the request unsatisfiable
measurementObjective: Given a prompt whose constraints conflict, identify which pair cannot both be met.
distractorStrategy: A constraint named that is merely demanding; the conflict located between two constraints that are compatible; the prompt declared satisfiable when it is not.

conceptName: Changing one thing at a time
factStatement: Revising several parts of a prompt at once leaves it unknown which change mattered.
familyName: Choosing the single revision that tests a hypothesis
measurementObjective: Given a hypothesis about why an output was wrong, choose the one change that would test it.
distractorStrategy: A rewrite that changes several things and would improve the output without explaining anything; a change that tests a different hypothesis; starting again from scratch.
notes: The most attractive wrong answer should be the one that plainly produces a better output, since that is the trade being measured.

factStatement: Given a stated requirement, prompts differ in whether their output could be accepted without rework.
familyName: Choosing the request that meets a stated requirement
measurementObjective: Given a requirement, choose the prompt whose output would satisfy it.
distractorStrategy: A prompt that is more detailed and misses the requirement; one that meets it and is unverifiable; one that would work for a slightly different requirement.
notes: The requirement must be stated precisely enough that exactly one prompt satisfies it.

factStatement: Goal, context, constraints, examples and output shape are what a request needs whatever the subject is.
familyName: Applying the parts of a request to an unfamiliar task
measurementObjective: Given a task in an unfamiliar domain, choose the request most likely to be answered usably.
distractorStrategy: A request that supplies domain detail and no task; one that states the task and omits the context the domain requires; one that would suit a familiar task rather than this one.
notes: The domain must be unfamiliar and fully described, so the item measures transfer rather than knowledge of the domain.

factStatement: Generated code is a proposal that has not been checked, however finished it looks.
familyName: Recognising what a generated suggestion has established
measurementObjective: Given a suggestion, say what its existence establishes about its correctness.
distractorStrategy: Compiling treated as evidence of correctness; a confident explanation treated as evidence; the suggestion dismissed as necessarily wrong, which is the mirrored error.
notes: The anchor family. Both over-trust and blanket refusal must be available as wrong answers.

conceptName: Whether it did what was asked
factStatement: Code can run correctly and do something other than what was requested.
familyName: Checking a suggestion against what was asked
measurementObjective: Given a stated requirement and a suggestion, say whether the suggestion meets it.
distractorStrategy: A suggestion accepted because it is well written; a suggestion rejected for a style difference rather than a behaviour difference; the mismatch located in the wrong part.

factStatement: A call that reads naturally may refer to something that does not exist, because plausible naming is what generation produces.
familyName: Recognising a reference that needs checking
measurementObjective: Given a suggestion, identify which part could not be trusted without being looked up.
distractorStrategy: A common construct flagged as suspect; the suspect call passed over because it reads naturally; the doubt attached to a value rather than to a name.
notes: Names are invented for the question rather than taken from any real library, so nothing here dates or rewards recall.

factStatement: Where a request left something unstated, the suggestion chose something without saying so.
familyName: Finding what a suggestion decided on its own
measurementObjective: Given a request and a suggestion, identify a decision the suggestion made that the request did not specify.
distractorStrategy: A decision named that the request did state; an assumption named that the code does not actually make; a style choice offered as an assumption.

factStatement: A suggestion generally handles the case described in the request and may handle nothing beyond it.
familyName: Identifying the case a suggestion does not cover
measurementObjective: Given a suggestion, name an input it would not handle correctly.
distractorStrategy: An input named that is handled; an input named that is outside the stated requirement; the omission described as a failure to run rather than a wrong result.
notes: Empty input, a single item and a duplicate are the productive cases and should recur.

factStatement: A doubt about a suggestion is answered by the input that would behave differently depending on whether the doubt is justified.
familyName: Choosing the test that would expose a stated doubt
measurementObjective: Given a specific doubt about a suggestion, choose the input that settles it.
distractorStrategy: A test that passes whether or not the doubt is justified; a test of a different property; running the original example again, which has already passed.
notes: This is the family that keeps the skill out of DEBUGGING: the fault is hypothesised rather than observed.

factStatement: Code that produces the right answer for the example given may be doing something that only coincides with the requirement.
familyName: Judging code that is right on the example
measurementObjective: Given a suggestion that matches the example, say whether it meets the requirement in general.
distractorStrategy: The suggestion accepted on the strength of the example; a general fault claimed where the code is in fact correct, so the family does not reward reflex suspicion.
notes: At least one stem in this family must have a genuinely correct suggestion.

factStatement: A suggestion can be sound in itself and wrong for the project it is being pasted into.
familyName: Judging whether a suggestion fits the project
measurementObjective: Given a described project and a suggestion, identify what makes it unsuitable here.
distractorStrategy: A mismatch named that the project description does not support; a real mismatch of naming style offered as though it were behavioural; the suggestion rejected as generally wrong.

conceptName: Checking the account against the code
factStatement: The description accompanying a suggestion is produced the same way as the code and can disagree with it.
familyName: Checking an explanation against what the code does
measurementObjective: Given code and its stated explanation, say whether the explanation is accurate.
distractorStrategy: The explanation accepted because it is coherent; a disagreement claimed where the two agree; the disagreement located in the wrong clause.

conceptName: What must be true before accepting
factStatement: Accepting a suggestion commits to it, so what must be checked first depends on what it would break if wrong.
familyName: Deciding what must be checked before accepting
measurementObjective: Given a suggestion and where it will be used, say what has to be established first.
distractorStrategy: A check proposed that is thorough and does not bear on this suggestion; the same check proposed regardless of consequence; acceptance on the grounds that it can be reverted.

factStatement: A generated fault is usually one that reads naturally, which is why reading alone does not find it.
familyName: Finding the fault in code that reads correctly
measurementObjective: Given a suggestion with a stated wrong result, identify the line responsible.
distractorStrategy: A line that is unusual and correct; the line where the wrong value becomes visible rather than where it arises; a line that would be wrong under a different requirement.

factStatement: A rewrite can alter behaviour nobody asked it to alter, and the alteration is not announced.
familyName: Finding what a rewrite changed beyond the request
measurementObjective: Given original code and a suggested rewrite, identify a behaviour the rewrite changed unasked.
distractorStrategy: A change named that was requested; a formatting difference offered as a behavioural change; a genuine change described as harmless when the stem shows otherwise.
notes: The unasked change should be one that improves something, since those are the hardest to notice and to argue against.

factStatement: A test that passes establishes that one input behaves correctly, and nothing about the inputs nobody tried.
familyName: Reasoning about what a check has established
measurementObjective: Given a check that has been carried out, say what it supports and what it leaves open.
distractorStrategy: The check read as establishing general correctness; the check dismissed as worthless; the conclusion drawn about a property the check never exercised.

factStatement: A task is safe to delegate in proportion to how cheaply a wrong result can be detected.
familyName: Deciding which task to hand to a generator
measurementObjective: Given several tasks, choose the one where a wrong result would be caught before it mattered.
distractorStrategy: A task chosen because it is tedious rather than because it is checkable; one whose failure is silent; one the student could not check at all, which is the worst case and often the most tempting.
notes: Every option must be a task a generator would attempt; only checkability separates them.

factStatement: Asking whether it meets the requirement, what it assumed, and what would expose the doubt works even where the student cannot read every line.
familyName: Judging a suggestion in unfamiliar territory
measurementObjective: Given a suggestion in a language or domain the student does not know, choose the step that reduces the risk most.
distractorStrategy: Asking the generator whether it is right, which produces another unverified claim; accepting because the code cannot be read; rejecting on the grounds of unfamiliarity alone.
notes: Asking the generator to confirm its own answer is the most attractive wrong option here and must appear.

factStatement: A fabricated detail is typically precise and well formed, because precision is what generation produces.
familyName: Recognising the kind of detail that needs checking
measurementObjective: Given an output, identify the element most likely to have been invented.
distractorStrategy: A vague statement flagged, where vagueness is not what fabrication looks like; a specific and checkable claim passed over because it looks authoritative.
notes: Precision reading as reliability is the belief this family exists to break.

conceptName: What must not be pasted in
factStatement: Material belonging to an employer, a client or another person leaves your control once it is sent somewhere else.
familyName: Recognising material that must not be sent
measurementObjective: Given several items, say which must not be pasted into an external service.
distractorStrategy: Public material flagged as confidential; genuinely confidential material passed over because it is only a fragment; the judgement made on volume rather than on ownership.

factStatement: Whether assistance must be declared depends on what the work was meant to demonstrate.
familyName: Recognising when assistance has to be declared
measurementObjective: Given a described piece of work, say whether assistance needs disclosing.
distractorStrategy: Disclosure treated as always required or never required; the judgement made on how much help was taken rather than on what was being assessed.
notes: Stated policies vary, so every stem states the policy and the measurement is applying it.

factStatement: A claim that will be acted on needs support in proportion to what acting on it wrongly would cost.
familyName: Deciding which claim most needs checking
measurementObjective: Given several claims in an output, choose the one that must be verified before use.
distractorStrategy: The most surprising claim chosen rather than the most consequential; a claim chosen that the reader could verify at a glance; every claim treated as equally urgent.

factStatement: A real source cited for a claim it does not make supports nothing.
familyName: Judging whether a source supports the claim it is attached to
measurementObjective: Given a claim and a described source, say whether the source establishes it.
distractorStrategy: A source accepted because it exists and is reputable; a source rejected for being informal though it says exactly the thing claimed; the mismatch located in the wrong part of the claim.
notes: Existing but not supporting is the interesting case and is harder to catch than a fabricated reference.

factStatement: Asking the same system again is not a check, because the second answer is produced the same way as the first.
familyName: Choosing a check that would settle a claim
measurementObjective: Given a doubtful claim, choose the step that would establish or refute it.
distractorStrategy: Re-asking the system, or asking it whether it is sure — the most attractive wrong answer; a check of a different claim; a check whose result would be consistent either way.
notes: Self-confirmation must appear as an option throughout; it is the habit this family exists to interrupt.

factStatement: A system reproduces the patterns in its examples, including patterns nobody intended it to learn.
familyName: Tracing uneven behaviour to its source
measurementObjective: Given a system that treats two groups differently, identify what would account for it.
distractorStrategy: Intent attributed to the system or its builders; the effect denied because no rule mentions the group; the cause located in the method rather than in the examples.

factStatement: Uneven treatment appears as a difference in output between cases that differ only in a way that should not matter.
familyName: Recognising an output that treats like cases differently
measurementObjective: Given two outputs for cases differing in one irrelevant respect, say what the difference shows.
distractorStrategy: A difference explained by a relevant factor the stem states; the difference dismissed as random variation where the stem rules that out; the finding overstated into a claim about every case.
notes: The two cases must differ in exactly one respect, or the item is not answerable from the stem.

conceptName: What must not be pasted in
factStatement: Once material has been sent, deleting the conversation does not undo the sending.
familyName: Reasoning about what follows once material has been sent
measurementObjective: Given material that has already been pasted in, say what can and cannot now be done about it.
distractorStrategy: Deletion offered as a remedy; the exposure treated as harmless because nothing visible happened; the remedy aimed at the tool rather than at telling whoever owns the material.

factStatement: Assistance is acceptable up to the point where it supplies the thing the work exists to demonstrate.
familyName: Deciding whether help crossed into substitution
measurementObjective: Given a stated purpose for a piece of work and the help taken, say whether the help was acceptable.
distractorStrategy: Help judged by quantity rather than by what it supplied; all assistance treated as substitution; help that supplied the assessed skill excused because the student read it afterwards.
notes: The stem must state what the work is meant to demonstrate, or the item collapses into opinion.

factStatement: An invented reference carries plausible authors, a plausible title and a plausible year, and refers to nothing.
familyName: Diagnosing a reference that does not exist
measurementObjective: Given a reference that cannot be found, say what follows and what to do.
distractorStrategy: The failure to find it blamed on access; the reference kept because the claim is probably true anyway; the system asked to supply the link, which produces another unverified claim.

factStatement: A claim that was never checked is repeated by everyone downstream, and the point at which checking was skipped is identifiable.
familyName: Locating where a wrong claim should have been caught
measurementObjective: Given a wrong claim that reached publication, identify the step at which it should have been stopped.
distractorStrategy: The generator blamed rather than the process; the last person to touch it blamed rather than the step that should have checked; a step named that had no means of catching it.

conceptName: Who is affected when it is wrong
factStatement: Whether an error matters depends on who bears it, which is often not the person who used the tool.
familyName: Reasoning about who bears the cost of a wrong output
measurementObjective: Given a use and an output that turns out wrong, say who is affected and how the risk should be weighed.
distractorStrategy: The cost assessed only for the user; the risk judged by how likely the error is without regard to its size; the harm treated as acceptable because the tool was clearly labelled.

factStatement: Whether to use the tool for a task turns on whether the output can be checked and on what a wrong output would cost.
familyName: Deciding whether to use the tool for a stated task
measurementObjective: Given a task with stated stakes, decide whether and how the tool should be used.
distractorStrategy: Use refused for a low-stakes checkable task; use accepted for a high-stakes uncheckable one; a conditional answer offered whose condition cannot be met.
notes: Both directions must appear. A student who always refuses has not learned to weigh anything.

factStatement: A policy written for known situations is applied to a new one by asking what it was protecting.
familyName: Applying a stated policy to a case it does not name
measurementObjective: Given a policy and a situation it does not mention, decide what it requires.
distractorStrategy: The case declared permitted because the policy does not name it; the policy read so broadly it forbids everything; the answer resting on a clause the stem does not contain.
notes: The policy is quoted in full in the stem, so the item measures application rather than recall of any institution's rules.
